text: Before you write a single gate, you need a working Python environment with the right packages installed, plus an IBM Quantum account if you ever want to leave the simulator and touch real hardware.

Install Qiskit into a dedicated virtual environment rather than your system Python, using venv or conda, to avoid version conflicts with other projects. Once it's active, pip install qiskit, qiskit-aer, and qiskit-ibm-runtime — the three packages from the previous lesson.

Open a Python shell inside your activated environment and check that Qiskit imports cleanly: print qiskit dot underscore underscore version. If that prints a version number without errors, your core install is good — you can do the same check for qiskit_aer and qiskit_ibm_runtime. An ImportError usually means you installed into one environment but are running Python from another.

To eventually run circuits on real hardware, you need a free IBM Quantum Platform account. Sign up, then find your API token and instance identifier on your account dashboard. The Platform's own header shows an account switcher and a region switcher, since the region controls where your jobs run and where their data is kept.

qiskit-ibm-runtime can store your credentials on disk with QiskitRuntimeService dot save_account, so you don't paste your token into every script. Never hardcode a real token into anything you'll share or commit. And one genuine caveat: IBM has changed its cloud authentication flow more than once, so check IBM's current documentation before you save your account rather than treating any tutorial's exact snippet as permanently frozen.

Next lesson draws a sharp line between two things that are easy to conflate: the Qiskit SDK you just installed, which is free and entirely local, and the IBM Quantum Platform, which is a separate cloud service with an account and usage limits.
